items.title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
items.summary: It marks the second attack on the country in three days and comes as the US and Iran remain locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz.
items.content:
Image caption, Iran and the US are vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz
Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.
The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.
Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".
It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.
The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.
Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.
As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.
Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."
In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."
Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.
The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.
Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

A Russian painting celebrates the upcoming meeting of Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. Photograph: Olga Maltseva/AFP/Getty Images
Anthony Albanese welcomes Trump-Xi-Putin summit – even as European leaders express reservations
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine
Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.
The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.
Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.
Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.
“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.
Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?
“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.
“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”
German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz , expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.
“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine , and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron , warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.
“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”
The meeting has been compared to a 1945 summit at Yalta , in southern Crimea, when then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe. Zelenskyy has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”.
The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.
“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.
“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”
Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.
“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.
After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo . It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.
More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

items.title: Warren Buffett stock market warning: What history reveals about crashes - Beinsure
items.summary: Warren Buffett stock market warning: What history reveals about crashes  Beinsure
items.content:
Warren Buffett stock market warning: What history reveals about crashes
Warren Buffett warns investors against speculative stock trading
Shiller CAPE ratio exceeds 40 as US stock valuations climb
What the 1929 crash, dot-com bubble and 2022 bear market reveal
Why high stock market valuations matter for future returns
Buffett's warning highlights the difference between price and value
Warren Buffett has warned that speculative behavior is becoming increasingly attractive to investors as US stock valuations reach levels rarely seen in history. His comments come amid renewed volatility across Wall Street, with the S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Dow Jones Industrial Average recovering after a difficult start to November 2026.
The warning coincides with the Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio rising above 40, a valuation threshold previously approached or exceeded during periods of extreme market optimism. Historical comparisons suggest elevated risks for long-term returns, although expensive markets can continue rising for extended periods.
Warren Buffett warns that speculative trading is increasingly replacing fundamentals-based investing as stock valuations climb.
The Shiller CAPE ratio has exceeded 40 in 2026, approaching levels associated with the dot-com bubble and other periods of extreme valuations.
Historical data links elevated valuations to weaker long-term returns, but the indicator cannot reliably predict when a stock market correction will begin.
Warren Buffett warns investors against speculative stock trading
During an interview with CNBC around Berkshire Hathaway's 2026 annual meeting, Buffett reiterated concerns about investors treating financial markets as a venue for short-term speculation rather than long-term business ownership (see Warren Buffett Retirement Income Strategy : Does the 90/10 Rule Still Work?).
"I've compared the markets to a church with a casino attached," Buffett said, distinguishing investment based on business fundamentals from trading driven primarily by price movements.
He warned that speculative activity had become particularly attractive, encouraging some market participants to accept risks without sufficient regard for underlying valuations. "That's not investing, it's not speculating, it's gambling," Buffett said.
His comments did not amount to a prediction of an imminent stock market crash.
Buffett also distinguished between excessive prices and the long-term value of owning productive businesses. He suggested that valuations across parts of the market could eventually appear difficult to justify.
"That doesn't mean that investing is terrible. It does mean that prices for an awful lot of things will look very silly."
The distinction matters because even companies with strong earnings growth can generate disappointing investment returns when their shares are purchased at excessive valuations.
Shiller CAPE ratio exceeds 40 as US stock valuations climb
The S&P 500 has recorded more than two dozen all-time highs during 2026, contributing to historically elevated valuation multiples.
One of the most widely followed measures is the Shiller CAPE ratio, which compares the inflation-adjusted price of the S&P 500 with the average inflation-adjusted earnings of its constituent companies over the preceding ten years.
Unlike conventional price-to-earnings ratios, CAPE uses a decade of earnings to reduce the influence of short-term changes in corporate profitability.
A reading above 40 indicates that investors are paying more than 40 times the index's average real earnings over that period.
Such valuations imply substantial expectations for future earnings growth and can leave share prices more sensitive to disappointing results, changes in interest rates or shifts in investor sentiment.
The Shiller CAPE ratio is a measure of valuation risk, not a market-timing indicator. It does not identify when prices will peak or how quickly a correction might develop.
High valuations can also reflect structural changes in the economy, including differences in corporate profitability, sector composition and investor expectations.
The increasing weight of large technology companies in major US indices is particularly relevant when comparing current valuation levels with earlier market cycles.
What the 1929 crash, dot-com bubble and 2022 bear market reveal
Historically, unusually high CAPE readings have coincided with periods preceding major stock market declines.
Before the 1929 Wall Street crash, US equities traded at elevated valuations as speculative demand pushed share prices substantially higher.
The subsequent market collapse helped mark the beginning of the Great Depression, although the economic downturn involved multiple financial and monetary factors beyond stock valuations.
During the late 1990s, enthusiasm for internet companies drove the CAPE ratio above 40.
The dot-com bubble subsequently burst, with technology stocks experiencing particularly severe losses as investors reassessed business models, earnings expectations and valuations.
Another significant valuation peak occurred in late 2021, shortly before US equities entered a bear market in 2022.
Rising interest rates, inflation and tighter monetary policy contributed to that downturn. These episodes demonstrate that high initial valuations can increase exposure to losses when market conditions deteriorate. They do not establish a consistent interval between a valuation peak and the beginning of a decline.
Markets have also remained expensive for years without immediately entering a sustained downturn.
Why high stock market valuations matter for future returns
The relationship between starting valuations and subsequent investment performance is generally more informative over long periods than over individual months.
When investors purchase shares at unusually high earnings multiples, future returns depend partly on companies generating sufficient profit growth to justify those prices.
If earnings fail to meet expectations, valuation multiples may contract even when businesses remain profitable.
This creates two separate risks: lower share prices during a market correction and weaker investment returns over subsequent years.
However, valuation measures cannot account for every factor influencing market performance. Corporate earnings, productivity, economic growth, monetary policy and investor demand can all affect equity prices.
For investors with long-term retirement accounts, elevated valuations are therefore a reason to examine portfolio concentration and risk exposure rather than assume that a market decline is imminent.
Buffett's warning highlights the difference between price and value
Buffett's investment philosophy has historically emphasized the relationship between the price paid for a security and the underlying economic value of the business.
His latest warning focuses on the risks of abandoning that distinction when markets are rising rapidly.
The Shiller CAPE ratio provides additional historical context by showing how expensive US equities have become relative to long-term corporate earnings.
Neither Buffett's remarks nor the valuation indicator establishes that a crash is inevitable in the near term.
The central risk is that investors paying unusually high prices may have less protection against earnings disappointments or changes in market sentiment, particularly when their portfolios are concentrated in stocks with elevated valuations.

Iran says 2 oil tankers hit mines near Strait of Hormuz, 1 sinks
Iran says 2 oil tankers hit mines near Strait of Hormuz, 1 sinks
Revolutionary Guard says sunken supertanker was carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil
Mustafa Melih Ahishali, Muhammet Torunlu and Rania Abushamala
ISTANBUL Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Sunday that two oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz, sinking one of the vessels.
The IRGC Navy said the tankers were attempting to use what it called an “unauthorized” route when the mine strikes triggered powerful explosions. It said one of the vessels, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, sank in the southern Gulf.
The force alleged that the tankers had switched off their navigation systems and tried to cross undetected with support from the US military.
The statement did not identify either vessel or give details on the crews.
Iran announced on July 12 that it had closed the strait again after the US resumed strikes on Iran. Tehran has warned it would target vessels that use routes other than those it designates or attempt to transit without its permission.
​​​​​​​The Strait of Hormuz is a major route for global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Disruptions to shipping through the waterway have heightened concerns over global energy supplies.

items.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
items.summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
items.content:
Image caption, The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Figure caption, Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

items.content:
Europe needs a warm winter to avoid major gas shortages – Chemicals and the Economy
Europe needs a warm winter to avoid major gas shortages
Europe needs a warm winter to avoid major gas shortages
Europeans need to hope that the forecasts of a Super El Nino prove correct. And that it means Europe will have a relatively warm winter:
Europe relies on natural gas to keep warm and keep its factories running in the winter
That requires it to store gas in the summer, before the winter starts
Its storage is meant to be 90% full today, as the Bloomberg chart shows
But in fact it is just 72% full – dangerously low
As TotalEnergies CEO, Patrick Pouyanné, has warned:
“It’s quite clear that we are entering a dangerous period. We have a world of crisis.”
Europe relies on imported gas in the form of LNG (Liquified Natural Gas).
Inevitably, prices are rising as the ICIS chart confirms:
One reason is the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, as that has shut off 20% of world supplies
A second reason is the decision to stop buying from Russia due to the Ukraine war
A third reason is the closure of Europe's largest gas field, Groningen, in 2023
It was causing small earthquakes as the underground gas was removed
The end result is that Europe is now competing with Asian countries for scarce US supplies. Asia is desperate for product as it has lost its normal Gulf supplies due to the Hormuz crisis.
Middle east crude oil flows rebound to pre-war levels
The risk of an LNG shortage has been obvious for some time. But markets and policymakers have focused instead on oil markets:
Hormuz-related shortages have been reducing in recent weeks as the Bloomberg chart shows
The Gulf countries have worked hard to restore supplies and create new supply routes
The world has also run down its emergency supplies close to ‘tank bottoms' as we noted in August
But as we have also noted, consumers don't use oil – they use oil products
There is thus a real risk that a cold winter will cause a major gas shortage, just as diesel and other products are also going short.
Diesel shortages have dropped off the news bulletins recently. But they haven't gone away as the IEA chart confirms.
Distillate stocks are at record low levels, and there seems little chance they will rebound soon.
Restarting Gulf refineries will take months, even if a peace deal can be agreed. Repairing damaged Gulf and Russian refineries will take years, due to the long lead times for replacement parts.
As Lakshmi Sreekumar, a member of the Dallas Fed Energy Advisory Council told ICIS last week:
"Between peak to trough, Middle East refinery runs dropped 30% between February and April. On top of that, Russian refinery runs from peak to trough dropped 28%."
“Those refined products are what really feeds into your consumer consumption system and also into inflation as well. It’s not just this one conflict…
"The Russia-Ukraine conflict on top of the Middle East conflict has made this refined products issue even worse.”
The risk is that we will all wake up one morning next year to find Europe and parts of Asia face major shortages of natural gas and refined products.
If we do, we will then all look back and wonder – "Why did nobody notice this until it was too late to do anything" ?

items.summary: The Fed’s battle against inflation risks turning into a forever war as Iran 'status quo' drags on  Fortune

The Fed’s battle against inflation risks turning into a forever war—and may last as long as Operation Iraqi Freedom while Iran ‘status quo’ drags on
Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a press conference following a Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, on October 28, 2026 in Washington, DC. Al Drago/Getty Images
In a few months, the Federal Reserve will be able to count six years that inflation has been above its 2% target, and central bankers’ own forecasts put “mission accomplished” sometime in 2029.
That means the Fed could fall short on the price-stability portion of its dual mandate for eight straight years—or as long as Operation Iraqi Freedom lasted.
Despite the obvious differences with the bloody Iraq war, the Fed’s inflation fight is also driven by events in the Middle East, this time in Iran.
Inflation was trending lower at the start of the year, as the initial spike from President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year was wearing off. Then crude prices soared after Iran closed off the Strait of Hormuz and attacked regional energy infrastructure in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes.
While oil exports have rebounded with the help of U.S. military protection, supplies of refined products like gasoline and diesel remain tight, inflicting more pain at the pump for consumers.
At the same time, GDP growth is running hot as the AI hyperscalers pour hundreds of billions of dollars a year into the economy, adding more pressure on prices.
This past week’s consumer price index for October came in hotter than expected and showed that inflation is spreading beyond energy categories into more goods and services, alarming Fed officials.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the data “borderline disturbing,” and fellow policymakers have indicated more rate hikes are needed, possibly even a jumbo-sized increase of 50 basis points.
Meanwhile, the Iran war shows no signs of ending soon. Trump has backed down from repeated threats to restart major combat operations, but has also shot down negotiations, saying the U.S. doesn’t need a peace deal with Iran.
“We’re just keeping it the status quo,” Trump told reporters on Monday.
With the Iran conflict dragging on indefinitely, the Fed may have to readjust its inflation outlook again and get more aggressive on rates.
In September, the Fed’s summary of economic projections put down 2029 as the year when inflation is expected to fall back to 2%, pushing it back from a 2028 forecast made in June, as energy prices stayed high.
To be sure, there have been several shocks outside the Fed’s control since inflation first exceeded 2% back in early 2021. The pandemic saw supply-chain snarls and massive fiscal stimulus. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 sent oil and gas prices soaring. Then came Trump’s trade war last year and his Iran war this year.
But the Fed has also provided monetary stimulus, and Chairman Kevin Warsh has argued that high inflation is a “choice,” suggesting shocks are no excuse. And the longer inflation stays above target, other central bankers have said they are less willing to be patient about rate hikes and “look through” short-term spikes.
Their fear is that an extended period of high prices will eventually cause consumers to lift their long-term inflation expectations and change currency spending patterns that fuel even more inflation.
That’s why the Fed has sounded more hawkish lately as policymakers look to ensure inflation expectations remain anchored and prevent consumers from believing there’s more tolerance for higher prices.
“I believe that the central bank has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility,” Goolsbee told CNBC on Friday. “We’ve been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we’re not making any progress, and if anything, it’s going the wrong way.”
On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller offered a similar message, saying a 50-basis-point rate hike should be considered at the Fed’s December meeting if October core consumer prices rose by 0.3% or more. In fact, they did rise 0.3% from the prior month.
“Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,” he explained.
Also on Tuesday, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said in separate remarks that it “may be possible to move more rapidly” than what September’s quarter-point hike and October’s hold have implied. She warned the ​current 3.75%-4.00% policy rate is too low and adds to inflationary pressures.
Diane Swonk, chief economist and managing director at KPMG, noted Fed hawks are coalescing as inflation has been too hot for too long—and moving higher.
“Fed is losing its inflation fighting credibility,” she posted on LinkedIn this week. “Consumers who rely mostly on wages, not their stock portfolios, are paying the price.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, right, and US envoy Jared Kushner, left, address members of the media after a meeting at Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel, west of Dublin, on November 12, 2026 [AFP]
US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to advance peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.
Kushner told reporters on Saturday that “both sides” – Kyiv and Moscow – know that compromises will be necessary to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were now working on the next steps.

US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a prisoner exchange .
The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders agreeing on Friday to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not believe it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.
The Kremlin has signalled openness to negotiations with Europe, but has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.
The five countries attending – France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom – have signalled a readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said that the Russian “acceptance, as it has been accepted by Jared Kushner of European participation [in the talks], is something that could actually be important”.
“Kushner makes direct reference as well to the issue of security guarantees required by Ukraine, and he makes clear that it would be NATO that would provide these guarantees,” Hanna said.
Moreover, he added, “as negotiators are suggesting, there might be another round of multilateral negotiations to build on what’s been called ‘substantial progress’ in the recent talks”.
In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said Europe must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.
Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.
Zelenskyy said on Friday that US negotiators had asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas, most of which Russia occupies, in exchange for joining NATO.
The war has raged while negotiations continue. November leaks from Russia’s official statistics agency showed that Moscow’s war effort has so far cost the lives of at least 450,000 soldiers.

Two killed in Leeds after car pursued by police crashes into another vehicle
Four arrested after BMW collides with Volkswagen on Gelderd Road, with police appealing for witnesses
Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police.
West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested after the crash in Leeds on Sunday and appealed for witnesses to come forward.
A force spokesperson said that at 12.44am a blue BMW 123D had failed to stop for a police vehicle in Gelderd Road, leading to a pursuit. The BMW then collided with a white Volkswagen Scirocco that was turning into Gelderd Road.
Police said the driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man from York, had been pronounced dead at the scene. A passenger in the same car, a 23-year-old woman from York, died in hospital a short time later. Neither has been formally named.
A 39-year-old man from Harrogate was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis in relation to the incident. He remains in custody.
Three other occupants of the BMW, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening. All three were arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.
West Yorkshire police have referred themselves to the Independent Office for Police Conduct, which has declared an independent investigation. A spokesperson for the IOPC said: “We have started an independent investigation after a fatal road traffic collision in Leeds following a pursuit involving West Yorkshire police.
“After we were notified by West Yorkshire police, we declared an independent investigation at around 2.30am and sent investigators to the scene and police post-incident procedure to begin gathering evidence.
The junction where the crash took place is surrounded by several car dealerships.
Pictures shared on social media overnight appeared to show an area around a segment of Gelderd Road cordoned off, with a fire engine and several police cars and ambulance vehicles in attendance. The pictures also appeared to show a dark car a short distance away from a very badly damaged white car just outside a used car dealership on Gelderd Road.
A cordon was still in place on Sunday morning with several officers in attendance, including a few inspecting the damaged cars. Drivers were advised to avoid the area.
Police appealed for witnesses and urged anyone with information or dashcam, mobile phone or CCTV footage to contact officers via 101 or online, quoting reference 13260649342.

How Will the Market React to a Potential Fed Rate Hike in December? Here's What History Suggests.
The Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates at its Dec. 9 meeting. CME FedWatch data indicated an 86.8% probability of a 25-basis-point (one-quarter of a percentage point) hike to 4%–4.25% and a 13.2% probability of a 50-basis-point (half percentage point) hike to 4.25%–4.50% during trading on Nov. 11.
Investors have already started reacting to changing rate expectations. After October inflation exceeded expectations, the two-year Treasury yield jumped about 18 basis points on Nov. 10. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) fell 0.38% on that day. However, the large-cap stock index rebounded 1.3% on Nov. 11, helped by a rally in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Image source: Getty Images. History shows that stocks do not always fall after rate hikes. The market's response also depends on what investors expect from the Fed's future interest rate decisions.
On Dec. 16, 2015, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25 basis points for the first time in nearly a decade. The S&P 500 gained 1.45% that day. Investors had anticipated the increase, and the Federal Reserve indicated that subsequent hikes would be gradual.
On Dec. 19, 2018, another 25-basis-points interest rate hike coincided with a 1.54% decline in the S&P 500. Investors were worried about slowing economic growth, while the Federal Reserve still projected additional interest rate increases. Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell also indicated that the central bank would continue reducing its bond holdings, a policy that withdraws liquidity from the financial system. This added to investors' concerns about tighter financial conditions.
However, the S&P 500 gained nearly 28% over the following 12 months, during which the Federal Reserve reversed course and cut interest rates three times in 2019.
The interest rate hike in March 2022 offers another example. The S&P 500 gained 2.24% on March 16, when the Federal Reserve began raising interest rates. However, the S&P 500 index lost 9.1% over the following 12 months, as inflation remained high and the central bank accelerated rate increases. The Russia-Ukraine war, slowing global growth, and recession fears also weighed on stocks.
These examples show why the market's immediate reaction to a rate hike does not necessarily indicate how stocks will perform over the following year.
A widely expected 25-basis-point hike in December may have a limited impact on stocks. However, a surprise 50-basis-point increase or signals of more rate hikes in 2027 could push Treasury yields higher and negatively impact stock prices.
In September 2026, Federal Reserve officials projected a median interest rate of approximately 4.1% at the end of both 2026 and 2027. The new projections in December 2026 could indicate whether policymakers now expect more increases. Higher interest rates can raise companies' borrowing costs and reduce what investors are willing to pay for their future earnings.
The pace of interest rate increases is also important. A Charles Schwab report examined 18 Federal Reserve tightening cycles since World War II. The S&P 500's average maximum 12-month decline following the first hike was 16% in faster-tightening cycles, compared with 12% in slower ones. These numbers measure the largest declines during those periods, not full-year returns.
The U.S. economy has remained resilient. Inflation-adjusted gross domestic product (GDP) grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter. Employers also added 165,000 jobs in October 2026. Continued economic growth could help companies sustain sales and earnings despite higher interest rates.
However, not all businesses can manage tight financial conditions. The Federal Reserve's May 2026 Financial Stability Report found that many publicly traded companies remained well positioned to service their debt. However, some riskier borrowers with floating-rate loans faced greater debt-servicing pressures.
Stocks trading at premium valuations may face downward pressure if investors are not willing to pay a premium for future growth. Instead, companies with strong cash flow and reasonable valuations may be better positioned to withstand further rate increases.
Investors hoping to avoid potential losses from a December rate hike may consider selling stocks before the Federal Reserve's announcement and buying them again at lower prices. However, this strategy requires accurately predicting when stocks will decline and when they will recover. Morningstar found that between January 1990 and March 2026, the median gap between the S&P 500's 10 worst and 10 best trading days was just seven days.
Historical returns also suggest that rate hikes do not necessarily lead to prolonged stock market declines. LPL Research examined six Fed tightening cycles since 1994 and found that the S&P 500 gained an average 6.7% in the 12 months following the first hike. However, the absolute returns varied across the different time periods.
A widely expected December rate hike may affect stocks, but unexpected signals about future increases could trigger volatility. Long-term investors may be better served by maintaining diversified portfolios and focusing on companies' financial health rather than trying to predict the market's immediate reaction.

Fed Rate Hikes Threaten U.S. Farm Margins as Debt Hits $605 Billion
The Fed signals more rate hikes as U.S. farm debt nears $605 billion, raising concerns over credit costs, shrinking margins and 2027 planting decisions.
Marcus Ellington is a U.S.-based journalist covering agricultural markets, global trade, and agricultural policy, with an international perspective on their impact across the global agri-food system.
Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins supported gradual interest rate increases on November 14, 2026 , citing persistent inflation and economic uncertainty. Her remarks, reported by Reuters, come as U.S. agriculture faces rising debt, elevated production costs and tighter operating margins. With the USDA projecting $605.1 billion in total farm debt for 2026 , additional monetary tightening could increase financing expenses just as producers prepare their 2027 planting budgets and investment decisions.
The Federal Reserve's benchmark interest rate currently stands at 3.75% to 4% , with markets anticipating another quarter-point increase at the December 8-9 meeting. Collins favors smaller, measured adjustments rather than aggressive tightening, although she acknowledged that economic data could change the policy outlook. For farmers, higher rates can translate into more expensive operating loans, machinery financing and farmland purchases, particularly for operations relying on variable-rate credit.
Bacteria and Fungi Boost Crop Yields by Nearly 15%, Analysis of 172 Studies Finds
Farm Debt and Input Costs Add Pressure to Agricultural Margins
According to the USDA Economic Research Service's September 2026 forecast, U.S. farm debt is expected to rise 4.6% to $605.1 billion , while production expenses could reach $492.8 billion, an increase of 4.5% . Net farm income is projected at $158.4 billion, down 2.6% in nominal terms. These figures highlight the financial pressure facing producers, although conditions vary considerably by commodity, region and farm size. Higher interest expenses could further reduce cash flow for operations already managing narrow margins.
Input inflation is adding another challenge. USDA projections indicate that spending on fertilizers, lime and soil conditioners could increase 15.3% in 2026 , while fuel and oil expenses may rise 28.8%. For corn, soybean and wheat producers, these increases complicate decisions about fertilizer purchases, equipment upgrades and acreage allocation. Agricultural cooperatives and input suppliers may also face higher working-capital costs, potentially influencing pricing, inventory management and financing terms offered to farmers.
The effect of higher rates depends on individual loan agreements. For example, a producer carrying $500,000 in variable-rate debt would pay approximately $1,250 more annually if the applicable interest rate increased by 0.25 percentage points and the outstanding balance remained unchanged. A half-point increase would add roughly $2,500. Actual borrowing costs depend on lender pricing, repayment schedules and loan structure, meaning Federal Reserve decisions do not automatically produce equivalent increases in agricultural loan rates.
Monetary tightening could also influence agricultural commodity markets. Higher U.S. interest rates may strengthen the dollar, making American corn, soybeans and wheat less competitive in some export markets. However, exchange rates are only one factor affecting commodity prices. Global crop yields, weather conditions, trade policies and international demand remain critical. For livestock producers, more expensive financing could affect herd expansion, feed purchases and investments in facilities, particularly when operating costs are already elevated.
December Fed Decision Raises Questions for 2027 Farm Financing
The Federal Reserve's December meeting will provide an important signal for agricultural lenders and producers preparing next year's budgets. Reuters reported that Collins considers gradual tightening appropriate because inflation remains above the Fed's 2% target , while higher long-term borrowing costs may already be restraining economic activity. The pace and extent of additional increases remain uncertain, with policymakers weighing persistent inflation against the risk of weakening economic growth.
Farmers entering the 2027 production cycle face decisions involving credit renewals, machinery purchases, fertilizer commitments and crop marketing. Variable-rate debt exposure, liquidity and debt-service costs are becoming increasingly relevant to those calculations. USDA Farm Service Agency lending programs, Farm Credit System institutions and crop insurance can support financial planning, although their availability and protection vary. For highly leveraged operations, even modest changes in financing costs may influence planting decisions and investment schedules.

Saudi, Iraqi Oil Replace Iranian Crude in China: Report
Saudi and Iraqi oil has begun replacing Iranian crude in China as Tehran's exports to the world's largest oil importer have plunged under the impact of a US blockade on its ports along the Arabian Gulf, imposed in July, Bloomberg’s Asharq Business website reported on November 15, citing vessel-tracking firm Vortexa.
Iranian oil exports to China fell to less than 100,000 barrels per day in October, down from around 1.4 million barrels per day before the war broke out in late February, Vortexa’s data showed.
The shift is creating an opportunity for major Gulf producers to expand their market shares in China, as the report said that Iranian inventories of crude loaded onto oil tankers and vessels used for floating storage, which Tehran had accumulated in the months before the war and the blockade, are now close to being depleted.
This is reducing its ability to continue meeting Chinese demand from available stockpiles, Vortexa argued.
Chinese buyers of Iranian crude have turned to Russian oil and other non-sanctioned grades, including Venezuelan crude, to make up for the loss of Iranian supplies, the firm added.
However, the firm said, these alternatives have not fully offset Iranian volumes, opening the door for Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and other Gulf producers to capture additional market share in China.

Iran says won’t remain in 'neither war nor peace' state
Iran says won’t remain in 'neither war nor peace' state
‘If the Americans accept our seven reasonable conditions, the path to an agreement remains open,’ Iranian parliament speaker says
ISTANBUL Iran will not remain in a state of "neither war nor peace," Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said Sunday, warning that Tehran was prepared for either negotiations or war with the US.
"If the Americans accept our seven reasonable conditions, the path to an agreement remains open," Qalibaf said at the opening of a virtual parliamentary session, as cited by the ISNA News Agency.
"However, if the Americans make another mistake this time, it will be the capabilities and determination of Iran's Armed Forces that determine the geographical scope of the battlefield, not their wishes or intentions," he warned.
Qalibaf did not elaborate on the seven conditions or provide details of what Iran would consider an acceptable agreement.
According to previous reports, Iran's seven conditions include lifting the US naval blockade, guaranteeing safe passage for commercial vessels and oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, removing unilateral sanctions, exempting Iranian oil exports from restrictions, releasing frozen Iranian assets, allowing Tehran to retain its nuclear materials inside the country, and ending the war.
His remarks came as he addressed the unveiling of a new missile facility, which he said had been built during the war and under enemy fire.
He described the facility as more than a technical or defensive achievement, saying it symbolized a shift in the region's strategic balance.
Qalibaf praised the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)’s Aerospace Force, saying its capabilities had challenged Israel and strengthened the morale of Iranians and supporters of the Palestinian cause.
The parliament speaker criticized recent remarks by the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, describing them as evidence of Washington's frustration with Iran's strength.
He said US officials should reflect on what he called their strategic failures in the Gulf rather than resort to insulting Iran.
His remarks came after Bessent recently used derogatory language about Iran's leadership and compared the IRGC to a “dangerous cornered animal” during a television interview. Bessent also said he had moved from his Washington residence to a military base because of security concerns.
Turning to domestic affairs, Qalibaf said economic challenges, particularly inflation, unemployment and price fluctuations, remained a major priority alongside military concerns.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran retaliated with strikes on Israel and US military facilities across the region before a ceasefire was reached in April.
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending the war. Efforts to reach a final settlement have stalled amid disagreements over freedom of navigation and security in the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy shipments and trade.

Donald Trump has pursued “the most idiosyncratic and unsuccessful” US foreign policy in living memory, said Max Boot in The Washington Post .
“Even among Republicans, there is little support for annexing Greenland , seizing Venezuela’s oil , waging a cold war with Canada , cutting off Ukraine, insulting and indiscriminately tariffing allies, buying diesel from Russia ” and “launching a war on Iran”. But most senior Republicans have been “too cowed” to protest, until now.
After last week’s “shellacking” in the midterms , Vice President J.D. Vance baldly stated on X that “the reason we lost is the war”. Trump himself had to admit that this is “largely true”; and this week, he said the war was “effectively over”, that negotiations to end it were under way, and that more attacks on Iran were “highly unlikely”.

Well, maybe, said Arta Moeini and Brett Erickson on UnHerd . But the president has been known to change his mind, and the danger of renewed conflict remains high. Trump is under “immense pressure to prove he is still in control”, and whatever constraints he now faces domestically, he retains considerable freedom to conduct foreign policy. A third aircraft carrier strike group is on course to reach the Middle East by the end of this month, building up the strength of US forces in the region to the level they were at at the start of the war.
Trump could attack Iran again, said Barak Ravid on Axios . But it would be “highly unpopular” – because it would drive oil prices up – and would probably not yield “a better military result”. The alternative is the peace negotiations. The difficulty is that Trump is making big demands: the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and the end of Iran’s nuclear programme . The Iranians are in no mood to make concessions. Tehran, according to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is asking not just for an end to the naval blockade and sanctions, but for billions in frozen assets, and reparations from the US.
There is a third option, said William Hague in The Times – for the US to carry on strangling Iran’s economy. With the last of the oil revenues from shipments sent out before the US blockade petering out, and inflation soaring, this is likely to be the most effective way of forcing Tehran to seek terms.
Trump will have to be patient, which does not come easily to him. He’ll also need to show that he can be trusted to honour any agreement; and he’ll probably have to accept some limited, independently verified Iranian nuclear activity. “Yes, that would look remarkably like the 2015 agreement that Trump hated so much.” But it is likely to be “the only path” out of the trap he has created for himself .

items.summary: Bessent has criticized Howard Lutnick’s department over suspected chip diversion to China while defending President Donald Trump’s handling of the matter.
items.content:
Bessent calls for ‘dramatic shakeup’ at Nvidia, urges outside CEO
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a “dramatic shakeup” at Nvidia and urged its board to hire an outside CEO following Jensen Huang’s resignation.
Bessent questioned whether Nvidia pursued potentially illicit chip sales to boost earnings and suggested other executives should face scrutiny.
The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, both of whom are expected to accompany President Donald Trump to China this week.
U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent speaks during a press conference in St. Cloud, Minn. on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings.
Bessent said Nvidia's board should look outside the company for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said in an interview on Fox News.
The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter.
Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit.
A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter.
Huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed , whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.
Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.
Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang.
"If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent said, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell.
Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a new methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales.

Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months.
The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place.
Lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners.
Cantor said Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said.
There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information.
Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China . Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut.
Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

As many as 100 Labour MPs could sign a letter opposing the giant Rosebank oilfield, as discontent among backbenchers looks likely to surge this week, with rebellions also brewing over Europe and welfare changes.
A total of 75 MPs have already signed the private letter, which is expected to be delivered in the next fortnight to Andy Burnham as part of a campaign in which Labour MPs from the party’s 2024 intake are playing a significant role.
While the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is said to be minded to reject the controversial oilfield, she could still be overruled by the prime minister, amid a cabinet split in which the chancellor, John Healy, is in favour of the plans.
The letter, first reported by the Sunday Times, says Britain’s credibility as a global climate leader would be destroyed if drilling went ahead off the Scottish coast, and argues that it would not reduce energy bills.
“We’re at a point where Reform and the Greens are on the back foot and Labour is enjoying a bounce, but a lot of people are very worried about Rosebank,” said one Labour MP who signed the letter.
“Andy’s big problem is also that he has let three fights start at the same time, which could prove to be very awkward. Rows about this and what our position should be on European relations have come at the same time as the debates that will come this week over [Alan Milburn’s] proposals on out-of-work benefits for young people. If control of the narrative on one issue is lost it could lead to panic about another.”
Another Labour MP said: “The interest in this is not just from the 2024 MPs. There are a good number of colleagues who just don’t sign letters like this normally, but who are concerned. It’s about staying true to what we told voters, and the fact that a lot of people after the summer we’ve had are really now making a link between the climate crisis and what their experience was when it comes to temperatures or flooding.
“The prospect of government resignations also looms if the drilling licence is granted. While the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is unlikely to go, such a decision would also put [him] in an awkward position given his past description of Rosebank as a ‘ colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism ’.”
A map showing the location of Rosebank and Jackdaw Instrumental in organising the letter is Sera, an affiliate and member-led environmental organisation within Labour, whose members include Miliband as well as ministers such as Luke Pollard, Georgia Gould, Matthew Pennycook and others.
Some who have signed the letter include those who had reluctantly backed the smaller Jackdaw field on the basis that it was primarily gas.
The company operating both fields said on Sunday that gas had begun to flow from the Jackdaw platform, “bringing vital UK energy resources ashore in time for winter”.
Claire Mueller, Jackdaw project director at the North Sea oil and gas producer Adura, said Rosebank and Jackdaw were expected to generate £1.4bn in tax revenues before the end of this parliament, rising to £3.8bn by the end of the next.
“With Jackdaw now producing, and other major projects including Rosebank in our pipeline, we have an opportunity to build a bright future for the North Sea, supporting jobs, investment and Britain’s energy security for years to come,” she added.
Miatta Fahnbulleh with Douglas Alexander (left), the Scotland secretary, and John Healey, the chancellor, on a visit to a gas terminal in Peterhead last month. Photograph: Paul Reid/PA Heavy backing for Rosebank is also coming from Labour-supporting unions the GMB and Unite, which have considerable influence over Burnham’s operation, and who are also expressing concern at his talk of rejoining the EU.
The letter opposing Rosebank is modelled on the one that derailed Keir Starmer’s welfare overhaul plans, which spanned the new intake and veterans. Yet one of its signatories pointed out stark differences.
“I do think it will probably get to around 100 MPs and may go beyond it, but the welfare rebels were willing to be much more ruthless. The other thing is that some of the people behind that rebellion are now in government and they are wise to these things.”
The government has described their process around Rosebank as “quasi-judicial”. Fahnbulleh previously told the Guardian that the decision would be consistent with the UK’s climate obligations, carbon budgets and the energy transition.

Share Give Donbas, take NATO seat: Could new US pitch work for Ukraine, Russia? on social media
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy answers media questions in Kyiv, Ukraine [File: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo]
The United States has pitched a new pathway for Ukraine to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), an aspiration that Kyiv has long held as a means to guarantee its defence against Russia, almost five years into their war.
But the administration of President Donald Trump has suggested that Ukraine would need to agree to give up all of the Donbas region in the country’s east, which Russian President Vladimir Putin has demanded as one of his conditions for ending the war.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 EU agrees on five countries to represent Europe in Ukraine peace talks
list 2 of 3 Car bombings in Russia kill military officer, injure ex-Ukraine PM adviser
list 3 of 3 Three killed in Russia as Ukraine claims US floated NATO membership option
The idea, according to Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, was communicated to him by Trump’s negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the latest round of US-mediated peace talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week.
After the Abu Dhabi round of talks, Kushner and Witkoff met Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then briefed Zelenskyy in Dublin, before a meeting of European leaders in the Irish capital on Friday.
Ukraine applied to become a member of NATO in September 2022, seeking to fortify its borders with Russia.
But the Kremlin has repeatedly said Ukraine becoming a member of NATO would demand “a harsh response” from Russia.
So will Washington’s latest pitch be acceptable to both Ukraine and Russia?
On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that Kushner and Witkoff had suggested that Ukraine could become a NATO member if it ceded control of Donbas in the east.
He said, “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'”
“NATO is back on the agenda” since it is part of an “extremely difficult” conversation between Ukraine and Russia which would determine the future of European security, Zelenskyy said.
Putin has been against Ukraine’s NATO membership and has demanded that the alliance pull back its troops from countries bordering Russia.
“This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.
“Real security in Europe means the EU [European Union] and NATO. That’s it. There is no other security in Europe.”
Ian Lesser, distinguished fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the US, told Al Jazeera that Washington’s proposal, if accurate, is significant because it articulates very directly an approach long current in US administration circles that Ukraine should be prepared to make territorial concessions in the service of a settlement.
“The NATO element seems very doubtful. Surely attractive to Ukraine, but [it is] hard to imagine Moscow agreeing to this. And some NATO members will be doubtful too,” he said.
Chris Featherstone, a political scientist from the University of York in the United Kingdom, argued that the proposal was a major departure from previously held positions.
“The US has been very cautious about getting further involved in Ukraine, with the Biden administration giving military support, but clearly opposing any ideas of Western involvement on the ground. Trump has seemed to be very sympathetic to the Russian cause, and has had significant blow-ups with Zelenskyy, so this proposal is certainly a surprise,” he noted.
He told Al Jazeera that offering NATO membership in a peace settlement would give significant support to Ukraine should Russia reinitiate the conflict in the future.
“In the light of Trump’s repeated attacks on NATO, this could be seen as a recommitment to the alliance. However, there would be questions over whether Trump could bring other NATO allies to support the proposal,” he added.
Ukraine applied to become a NATO member in September 2022, just months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the country.
Since then, Zelenskyy, his officials and Ukrainians around the world have been lobbying NATO nations to speed up Kyiv’s accession process.
But NATO members remain divided over offering Ukraine alliance membership amid an ongoing war despite a broad consensus to signal strong support for Kyiv.
NATO members bordering Russia, like Lithuania and Poland, have been most enthusiastic about backing Ukraine’s ambitions. Several other nations in the alliance have also been supportive of an expedited process for Kyiv to join, amid concerns about corruption in Ukraine and while seeking an end to the war with Russia as a condition for the country to become a NATO member.
But under President Trump, the US has been far less receptive to Ukraine’s calls for NATO membership. Trump has publicly told Ukraine to give up on hopes of joining the alliance.
Yet, while the new proposal from Witkoff and Kushner revives Ukraine’s hopes of joining NATO, it demands a compromise that no government in Kyiv can easily make.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that the prospect of Ukraine joining NATO in exchange for ceding territory had not been raised by members of the alliance before and reiterated that Kyiv would not give up any of its territories.
But he said if Ukraine received a peace deal which included security guarantees, the right to maintain a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army, and funds to rebuild the country, then he would hold a national referendum on the question of ceding territory in exchange for NATO membership.
Featherstone noted that Ukraine has been fighting for a long time and has consistently maintained that it will not relinquish its territory in a peace deal.
“The proposal from the Trump administration is clearly an attempt to test this Ukrainian position, in an effort to confront the impasse,” he said.
“NATO membership would give a level of security that Ukraine would likely welcome. However, this would be a big sacrifice of territory and sovereignty. After years of Trump’s questioning of the NATO commitment, Ukraine would need a strong statement of commitment to its defence should they be considering any proposal like this,” he added.
The Kremlin has not yet responded to the latest US proposal.
But it has maintained a strict position that Ukraine’s NATO membership is a red line for Moscow and a direct threat to Russia’s national security. In fact, Putin has also cited the issue of Ukraine’s NATO aspirations as one reason why Russia launched its war in 2022.
Despite Kushner and Witkoff’s meetings with Putin, the Kremlin has shown little appetite for a change in that position. Moscow has continued, throughout the war, to demand that Ukraine abandon its NATO ambitions and maintain a neutral and demilitarised status. Russia has also firmly opposed any deployment of Western troops or peacekeepers on Ukrainian soil.
In addition to demanding that Ukraine give up its NATO dreams, Moscow has also insisted that Ukraine should cede sovereignty over the Donbas region, in addition to parts of Zaporizhia and Kherson provinces that Russia already occupies.
Just as the new US proposal asks Ukraine to give up some territory in return for a NATO seat, it offers Russia a bargain — withdraw its red line on Ukraine’s NATO membership and get the Donbas in exchange.
The region in eastern Ukraine has historically been the country’s industrial heartland and is therefore a critical economic engine.
A majority of people in the Donbas identify as ethnically Ukrainian, but a minority identifies as ethnically Russian. The Russian language is also widely spoken in the region — a legacy of Russian migration there in the 19th century and then under the Soviet Union.
Russia accuses Ukraine of discriminating against Russian-speaking and ethnically Russian people in the Donbas and has used this claim to justify its demand that Kyiv hand over the region to Moscow.
The region consists of the provinces of Luhansk and Donetsk. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has occupied almost all of Luhansk and most of Donetsk. In all, it controls about 88 percent of the Donbas region. But it has consistently demanded that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the remaining parts of the Donbas they currently hold.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director of geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, who previously served on the NATO secretary-general’s policy planning staff, told Al Jazeera the US proposal tests the extent to which the territory of Donbas really matters to Russia.
But he said the recent Abu Dhabi talks had shown that Russia wanted more than just territorial concessions from Ukraine.
“They [the Russians] want to discuss what they call a new European security architecture, which is a code name for Russia having veto [power] when it comes to NATO,” he said.
He noted that it was also interesting that the Americans did not put forward the idea of Kyiv ceding the Donbas to the Russians in exchange for NATO membership.
“But everything indicates that the Russians will never accept this,” he said, referring to the idea of Ukraine joining NATO.
“The Russians have no intention of actually coming to the negotiating table. They’re just bringing up new issues [currently about European security architecture] and broadening the agenda in order to make it look like they’re negotiating and appease the American leadership, while inflicting as much damage on Ukraine as possible,” he added.
The US has not explicitly announced that it has suggested Kyiv should cede territory for NATO membership.
On Saturday, hours after Zelenskyy’s remarks to reporters, in a lengthy post on X, Kushner suggested that “the press has reported some of the maximalist positions proposed by both sides, along with strong political rhetoric”.
He highlighted that the conversations between Russia, Ukraine and the US were “private discussions” aimed at ending the war.
“Several new ideas emerged from these discussions and are now being explored. Some may lead to breakthroughs directly, while others may evolve into new proposals that help bridge the remaining gaps,” he said.
“In our private discussions, both sides understand that practical compromises will be necessary to end this war. Serious and constructive work continues among those of us committed to finding solutions,” he added.
Earlier, on Thursday, Kushner also told reporters that Putin has agreed to include Europe in peace negotiations.
“We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” he said.

Prince Harry meets wounded veterans at the National Invictus Games in Lviv [Lviv Oblast Military Administration handout via Al Jazeera]
Britain’s Prince Harry has met wounded veterans and medics in Ukraine during a surprise visit.
The royal family member attended Ukraine’s National Invictus Games and a conference for medics in the western city of Lviv on Saturday. It was organised by Superhumans, a clinic that specialises in the rehabilitation of war-wounded.

list 2 of 3 Three killed in Russia as Ukraine claims US floated NATO membership option
list 3 of 3 Starshield restrictions help Russia’s energy attacks on Ukraine: Zelenskyy
“Every single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth,” Harry said, adding that he’d “taken a risk to come here”.
Ukraine has about 1.4 million combat veterans, more than 10 percent of whom have disabilities.
“You’re going to win the war,” the 42-year-old British royal said during his fourth trip to the country since the start of the conflict with Russia in 2022.
Prince Harry at Ukraine’s National Invictus Games in Lviv [Credit: Lviv Oblast Military Administration handout via Al Jazeera] The prince watched wheelchair rugby players competing for a place in Ukraine’s team for next year’s Invictus Games in Birmingham in England.
Around 500 people have registered to compete to qualify for the 60-member squad – the largest ever team – that Ukraine is planning to send to the 2027 event.
“You’re going to win the war and then you’re going to be set up for success,” he said.
Prince Harry is the founder and patron of the Invictus Games Foundation, which he established in 2014 to support wounded, injured and recovering military service personnel and veterans through adaptive sports, e-sports and recovery programmes.
“When the war is over and when Ukraine wins, we will be ready to support you in holding an Invictus Games,” Harry told wounded veterans later on Saturday.
Prince Harry at the National Invictus Games in Ukraine [Credit: Lviv Oblast Military Administration handout via Al Jazeera] At a rugby game, he hugged Valery Odainyk, a contestant at the Invictus Games in Canada last year. The leg amputee is “still an active serviceman” in the Ukrainian forces.
“So when do you find time to train?” Harry asked in surprise.
The 41-year-old Odainyk said he told Harry that his involvement in disability sport “all started and continues with the Invictus Games.”
They feature a mix of adaptive core and winter sports, such as alpine skiing, archery, track and field, cycling, wheelchair basketball, rugby and tennis.

Ukrainian forces have struck at least six bridges along a major Russian logistics corridor since early October, damaging transport links connecting Russia’s Rostov region with occupied southern Ukraine, including routes used to supply Russian forces in Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, and Crimea.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi on November 15, citing the OSINT monitoring group Oko Gora, the strikes targeted railway and highway bridges in Russia’s Rostov region and near occupied Novoazovsk in Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
Map showing bridges struck by Ukrainian forces since early October 2026 along Russia’s key supply route to occupied southern Ukraine. (Source: Oko Gora)
The attacks have affected several sections of the R-280 highway corridor, a major transportation route linking Rostov-on-Don with temporarily occupied Mariupol, Berdiansk, Melitopol, and Crimea. The first reported strikes occurred on October 10, when Ukrainian drones targeted two bridges across the Don River in Rostov-on-Don.
One drone struck the operating mechanism of a railway drawbridge on the Rostov–Bataysk line. A separate attack damaged the combined road and railway Western Bridge. Neither crossing sustained critical damage, and traffic resumed shortly afterward.
A further strike on November 8 damaged a bridge across the Mius River near Nataliivka on the R-280 highway.
Map showing Russia’s R-280 logistics corridor linking occupied Mariupol with Crimea through Melitopol and Berdyansk. (Source: Oleksandr Manulians/UNITED24 Media)
The governor of Russia’s Rostov region confirmed damage to the roadway and two crawler cranes involved in reconstruction work. The bridge had been undergoing expansion to four lanes when it was attacked.
Traffic was initially suspended, although local traffic authorities reported that limited movement resumed on November 14 using a temporary bridge with alternating one-way traffic. On November 11, Ukrainian forces also reportedly inflicted critical damage on a bridge near Huselshchykove, close to temporarily occupied Novoazovsk.
The crossing had served as an alternative to another bridge over the Hruzkyi Yelanchyk River, which was undergoing repairs following earlier Ukrainian strikes.
Category War in Ukraine Inside Ukraine’s Logistic Lockdown
The closure reportedly complicated road transportation between Russia’s Rostov region and temporarily occupied southern Donetsk region, potentially forcing vehicles to travel an additional 150 kilometers (93 miles).
The latest attacks occurred overnight on November 15, when drones struck two more crossings in the Rostov region. One attack damaged a highway overpass above railway tracks in the Neklinovsky district, prompting authorities to close the crossing.
Another strike targeted a bridge across the Mius River near Mykolaivka, north of the crossing attacked on November 8. Photographs published following the attack appear to show the bridge completely destroyed.
The R-280 highway, which Russian authorities call the Novorossiya highway, incorporates sections of Ukraine’s M-14 and M-18 highways alongside local roads. The corridor connects Rostov-on-Don with Russian-occupied territories along the Sea of Azov and provides an important overland supply route toward Crimea.
Category War in Ukraine Ukraine Changed the Battle for Crimea. Russia Is Running Out of Ways In
According to Militarnyi, restrictions on freight transportation across the Crimean Bridge, combined with previous Ukrainian missile and drone strikes against ferries and cargo vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, have increased Russia’s dependence on the R-280 corridor.
The outlet describes the highway as effectively the only remaining major logistics route supporting Russian transportation to and from Crimea, as well as a principal supply corridor for temporarily occupied areas of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported a record of more than 41,000 verified strikes against Russian troops in October, with nearly 24,000 Russian personnel reportedly killed. Since the beginning of 2026, Ukrainian forces have confirmed strikes against more than 320,000 Russian troops.
