items.content:
Nvidia Chip Loophole: 240,000 GPUs, $7.5B Claim Unproven
Photo: Lawrence Systems, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons Nvidia is dealing with two stories at once, and each one feeds the other. The first is personal. CEO Jensen Huang told employees in an email that he had been "unfaithful to my wife," and reporting has connected the affair to Alice Huang , also reported as Huang Le, a businesswoman associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed International. The second is structural, and it matters far more to the AI industry. The fallout has put a spotlight on the Nvidia chip loophole that lets Chinese companies reach high-end GPUs without an obvious break in the rules.
On Nov. 14, CNN Business reported that the scandal has lifted the curtain on a loophole giving China access to US chips. Reports also describe a second, far more serious channel: the alleged diversion of restricted semiconductors. That second claim is where the legal risk sits. The US investigation into Megaspeed had not reached a conclusion in the cited reporting, and Megaspeed and related parties deny any link to illegal diversion. Our earlier report on the Shanghai side of the Megaspeed network covers the procurement angle in more detail.
This analysis separates what has been reported from what has been proven. It explains how the remote-access route works, sizes the claims against the numbers on the record, compares the competing access paths, and looks at what the story means for AI model development in both countries. Every allegation below is labeled as an allegation. Where a figure is unconfirmed, we say so.
Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
What Happened: The Nvidia Chip Loophole Behind the Huang Affair Story
The affair headline grabbed attention first. The business question underneath it is harder to dismiss. The Washington Post and other outlets have raised the question of whether a personal relationship between Nvidia's chief executive and a figure tied to one of its Southeast Asian customers created a blind spot in how the company watched who ended up using its most valuable products.
Nvidia has answered that part directly. The company said its internal investigation had found no information indicating that Jensen Huang exchanged confidential business secrets with Alice Huang. That statement is narrow. It addresses the sharing of secrets and says nothing about whether the customers in question complied with export rules. It also does not settle the separate question of how chips traveled from authorized buyers to Chinese end users.
Three claims keep getting blended together in social media posts, and they should stay apart. The first is that a personal relationship existed, which Huang's own email acknowledged in general terms. The second is that the relationship helped move chips to China. The third is that Chinese firms used a network of intermediaries to get around export controls. The second and third claims are unconfirmed allegations. So are claims that Alice Huang acted as a Chinese intelligence asset. No court or regulator has ruled on any of them.
A short list of items can be stated with confidence because the reporting supports them directly. Nvidia and Jensen Huang are named in the coverage. Megaspeed International is a Singapore-based cloud-computing company and an Nvidia customer. Alice Huang is associated with that company. A Malaysian subsidiary called Speedmatrix has been linked in reporting to Megaspeed's network. And Huang's email to employees included the admission that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without further detail.
Everything beyond that list carries qualifiers. The table below sorts the main claims by how firmly the reporting supports them. We built it from the reporting available as of Nov. 15, 2026, and we will treat any status change as news when it happens.
Huang told employees he was unfaithful to his wife Reported, from his own email AFP, Business Insider
Nvidia's internal probe found no sign Huang shared confidential business secrets Nvidia's stated finding Nvidia, via news reports
About 240,000 H100, H200 and some A100 chips moved into China Reported, not independently established Reporting by The Information and others
At least $7.5 billion in chip shipments to China Unconfirmed allegation The Information
Alice Huang acted as a Chinese intelligence asset Unconfirmed allegation Multiple outlets, denied by Beijing
The relationship enabled the shipments Unconfirmed allegation Multiple outlets
Alibaba or other Chinese firms knowingly joined illegal diversion Unconfirmed allegation Multiple outlets
US probe into Megaspeed diversion has concluded False so far, still open Cited reporting
Alice Huang goes by Huang Le in some reporting. Outlets describe her as a businesswoman with a senior role tied to Megaspeed International, either current or former depending on the account. Megaspeed is a cloud-computing company based in Singapore and counts as an Nvidia customer. Its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, appears in reporting about the wider regional network.
Cloud companies in Southeast Asia occupy a legitimate and growing slot in the AI supply chain. They buy large GPU clusters, house them in local data centers, and rent capacity to customers who cannot or do not want to build their own. Singapore and Malaysia both appear in the reporting on this network. A cloud partner with a strong relationship to Nvidia can win fast access to the newest hardware, which makes its customer list a matter of real consequence.
That is why the Megaspeed link drew attention so quickly. Investigators and reporters do not treat a Singapore cloud provider as suspect by default. The concern is about what sits behind it. Reports raise questions about ownership, about who the end users were, and about whether chips stayed in the facilities where they were first installed. Megaspeed rejects the framing. The company said it takes export control laws seriously and has cooperated with US inspections.
We also looked at the security side of the story in our piece asking where Nvidia's security team was as the Megaspeed relationship developed.
How the Nvidia Chip Loophole Works: Renting Versus Shipping
US export controls restrict the sale and transfer of advanced AI chips to Chinese buyers. They focus on hardware moving across borders. The loophole that DW and other outlets have examined exploits that focus. A Chinese company does not need to import a GPU if it can rent time on one that sits in a data center in another country. The chip never crosses into China, but the compute still serves a Chinese customer.
Reports describe Chinese AI labs and large technology companies renting capacity from overseas providers. Alibaba and Tencent appear in reporting as end users served by some of the chips, along with smaller Chinese AI laboratories. Whether this kind of renting violates US rules depends on how the rules are written and enforced, and the reporting treats it largely as a gap rather than a clear violation. Claims that Alibaba or other named Chinese companies knowingly took part in illegal diversion remain unconfirmed.
The second route is a different matter. Diversion means buying chips through a front or intermediary and then moving them to a buyer who could not have bought them directly. It is the conduct US investigators look for when they examine a cloud customer. The investigation into Megaspeed concerns alleged diversion or smuggling of restricted semiconductors. Megaspeed and related parties deny any connection to it.
The distinction matters for readers who see headlines that say "Nvidia chips smuggled to China." Hosting chips abroad and renting them out is an ordinary business, even when the renter is Chinese. Moving restricted chips into China without a license is a violation. Mixing the two lets people claim too much in either direction.
The 240,000-Chip Figure and the $7.5 Billion Allegation
Two numbers dominate the coverage. Approximately 240,000 Nvidia H100, H200 and some A100 chips were reported as having moved into China. Separately, at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to China was reported as an allegation attributed to The Information. Our earlier analysis of why US chip curbs failed used a different dataset, so readers should not add these figures together or treat them as one measurement.
Reuters carried the $7.5 billion claim as a report from The Information, and it fits the pattern of an allegation rather than a finding. The figure has no independent confirmation, and the reporting does not say whether it covers chips, equipment, or services. Treat it as the upper end of what investigators may be examining rather than a sum anyone has proven.
The 240,000 figure has a similar caveat. It describes chips reported as moved into China, but reporting does not break that total down by route. A chip hosted in Malaysia and rented to a Chinese lab counts differently under the law than a chip physically delivered to Shanghai. Without that split, the headline number cannot tell readers how much of the flow was legal and how much was not.
Even so, the scale deserves attention. A fleet of 240,000 H100-class and H200-class accelerators, if the reports hold up, would represent serious training capacity. These are the chips that power frontier-scale model development. The figures do not prove wrongdoing by any named company. They do show why Washington cares about a gap that looked minor in earlier years.
Shanghai Century Litong and the Preferred Cloud Partner Question
One company in the reporting gives the loophole story a concrete shape. Shanghai Century Litong is a China-based company reportedly founded in June 2023. Reports say it obtained Nvidia "preferred cloud partner" status by October 2023. That timeline is short, roughly four months from founding to a status that signals a close commercial relationship with Nvidia.
Speed alone proves nothing. Fast-growing firms do sometimes win partner status quickly, especially in a market where Nvidia wants distribution. What the timeline does is raise a due-diligence question. How closely did Nvidia vet a young company with a Chinese base before granting a status that could ease access to supply? The reporting does not answer that, and Nvidia has not publicly walked through its vetting process.
The question also connects back to the central scandal. If personal relationships between executives and customer-side figures shaped who got access, investigators will want to know whether normal compliance checks ran as designed. The company's internal investigation, and the outside review we covered in our look at the board-level probe and its missing timetable , will have to answer that. Neither has issued public findings on partner vetting.
The direct statements so far come from four parties. Each is quoted below exactly as published, with the source linked. Huang's apology to staff, relayed by AFP , read: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did."
On the business side, Business Insider attributed a statement to Huang from a Bloomberg interview: "Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual." That sentence ties the relationship to Megaspeed directly, which is why it drew attention. It is also a defense, since Huang describes the dealings as ordinary.
When Nvidia announced an independent investigation, CNBC reported that Huang said: "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."
The other two parties spoke through Reuters on Nov. 12. Megaspeed International said: "Megaspeed takes export control laws seriously and has cooperated with U.S. inspections." The Chinese government's position, as Reuters summarized it: "Beijing calls the spying claim a groundless accusation, slander and a smear." Both statements are denials, and neither resolves the factual questions. They do set the terms for the dispute ahead.
Historical Context: Why Export Controls Target Hardware
The remote-access gap exists because of how Washington built its restrictions. The earliest controls on advanced AI chips targeted physical products. Officials could count GPUs, set performance thresholds, and require licenses for shipments. That approach worked reasonably well when the main worry was a Chinese buyer importing a server rack.
Cloud computing changed the picture. A GPU cluster in another country can serve users anywhere, and the service moves through ordinary internet connections. The law has to decide whether renting access counts as an export of the capability. The Megaspeed episode puts that question back on the table with a high-profile example.
A second pressure point came from enforcement. Controls on paper depend on customs checks, license reviews, and company-level compliance. Each layer has limits, and a determined intermediary can exploit the seams between them. Fortune tackled this theme in its Nov. 10 piece, which framed two separate scandals as converging on the same China smuggling allegations, and the argument is a fair read of why this story will not fade quickly.
Finally, policy debates shape enforcement. Supporters of tighter limits argue that every gap undermines the rules, while industry voices warn that heavy restrictions push Chinese buyers toward domestic suppliers. The Megaspeed case hands the first group a fresh argument.
Competitive Comparison: Three Ways Chinese Firms Reach Nvidia Compute
Chinese AI developers have three broad options for getting high-end Nvidia compute. The table compares them on legal footing, visibility to regulators, and the main risk each poses. The comparison reflects the reporting described above, and it uses no unpublished figures.
Route How it works Legal footing in reporting Main risk
Remote access to overseas GPUs Chinese firm rents capacity in data centers in places like Singapore or Malaysia Treated as a gap in the rules, not a clear violation Rule change closes the gap
Physical diversion through intermediaries Restricted chips bought by a front or partner then moved into China Illegal if proven, still alleged Criminal and civil enforcement
Domestic Chinese accelerators Buyer uses chips made in China Fully legal Lower performance, software gaps
Licensed direct purchase of permitted chips Buyer purchases models cleared for sale to China Legal under current licenses Weaker hardware than restricted parts
The table shows why remote access draws so much attention. It combines strong hardware with a legal grey area and low visibility. By contrast, physical diversion carries high legal risk and, once uncovered, produces clear evidence trails. Domestic chips sidestep the legal problem but sacrifice performance. That tradeoff explains why firms chase the first two routes despite the risk.
Market Impact: Nvidia, Cloud Providers and Chinese AI Labs
Nvidia faces the most direct exposure. The company has sold a large share of its data-center products to a small number of big buyers, and any hint that its distribution network leaks into restricted markets invites regulatory attention. Investors now watch for stricter reporting rules on cloud partners, tighter end-use checks, and possible limits on who can buy the newest products. Any of those changes could slow sales to otherwise legitimate customers.
Nvidia's compliance posture will likely become part of how analysts value the company. A firm that can show tight control of its channel earns more trust from regulators. A firm that cannot may face rules that cut into revenue at the margin. We have not seen figures on that effect, and we will not estimate one here.
Providers in Singapore and Malaysia may feel the pressure next. If regulators decide that renting GPU time to Chinese customers needs a license or end-user screening, every provider in the region will have to add compliance staff and customer checks. Smaller operators could struggle with the cost. Larger ones may see it as a chance to win business from firms that cannot meet the new bar.
Chinese laboratories that rely on overseas rented compute face the biggest strategic risk. A rule change could cut off access quickly, and domestic alternatives still trail the best Nvidia parts. Large firms such as Alibaba and Tencent can absorb disruption better than smaller labs. The smaller labs have the thinnest margin for error and may have to shrink training runs or delay releases.
This story sits squarely in the AI models beat because compute decides which models get built. Training a frontier model takes thousands of high-end accelerators running for weeks. A lab that loses access to such clusters will fall behind the labs that keep it. Our AI and machine learning coverage tracks that link between hardware access and model releases.
Several of our recent reports touched the same question from the model side. One looked at reports tying six Chinese AI models to Blackwell hardware with the training location unknown . Those stories and this one share a gap in the evidence. Observers can see a model's output, but they usually cannot see where it trained or on whose chips. That gap lets each side argue its case without proof.
For researchers and engineers outside China, the practical effect is indirect. Tighter rules on cloud access could change pricing and availability for everyone who rents GPUs in Southeast Asia. Compliance paperwork may slow onboarding. Developers who use these providers for legitimate work should watch their vendors' announcements about customer screening.
The bigger lesson concerns evidence. The public cannot verify which Chinese models trained on which chips, and the Megaspeed case shows how hard it is for investigators too. Until regulators get better tools for tracing compute, claims about banned hardware in specific models will stay hard to prove and hard to dismiss.
Timeline: From 2023 Partner Status to the November 2026 Probe
The table below lays out the dated events in the reporting. It includes only items the sources support, and it leaves out dates we could not confirm.
June 2023 Shanghai Century Litong reportedly founded Reported
October 2023 Shanghai Century Litong reportedly holds Nvidia preferred cloud partner status Reported
Nov. 8-9, 2026 Nvidia announces an independent investigation, with Huang pledging cooperation CNBC
Nov. 10, 2026 Reuters relays The Information's $7.5 billion shipment allegation Allegation, unconfirmed
Nov. 12, 2026 Megaspeed says it cooperated with US inspections, Beijing rejects spying claim Reuters
Nov. 14, 2026 CNN Business details the loophole giving China access to US chips CNN
The dates show a story that moved fast. Within a week, the personal admission, the corporate investigation, the denials, and the policy analysis all arrived. That pace helps explain why so many claims circulate without confirmation. Reporters and readers are still sorting out what happened while new items keep landing.
These are our analysis, not reported facts. They rest on the pattern of the story so far.
Remote access draws a formal policy response. The loophole is now the main thread of the coverage, and lawmakers in both parties have reason to act. Expect proposals that require licenses or end-user screening for overseas GPU rentals.
Nvidia tightens cloud-partner vetting. The company has strong incentives to show regulators it controls its channel. Look for new partner audits and stricter conditions for preferred status.
The Megaspeed probe stays open for months. Export investigations rarely move fast, and the cited reporting shows no conclusion. A quick resolution would surprise us.
The $7.5 billion figure either shrinks or gets a firmer source. Allegations of this size usually face scrutiny from other outlets and from regulators. Either outcome will change how the story reads.
Chinese labs push harder on domestic chips. Even a hint of lost access raises the cost of relying on rented Nvidia compute. The case adds momentum to domestic alternatives.
The takeaway: the affair supplied the headline, but the loophole supplies the lasting policy question. Whoever answers it will shape who can train the next generation of AI models.
Reports describe it as the ability of Chinese companies to use Nvidia GPUs hosted in other countries, such as data centers in Southeast Asia, without importing the chips into China. US restrictions focus on physical shipments, so renting remote capacity falls into a gap. CNN Business and DW have both examined the mechanism.
Alice Huang, also reported as Huang Le, is a businesswoman associated with Megaspeed International. Reporting has linked her to Jensen Huang's admitted infidelity. Claims that she served as a Chinese intelligence asset are unconfirmed, and Beijing has called the spying claim a groundless accusation.
Nvidia said its internal investigation found no information indicating that he exchanged confidential business secrets with Alice Huang. That is the company's stated finding, and an independent investigation was announced separately.
Reports put the figure at approximately 240,000 H100, H200 and some A100 chips. A separate allegation attributed to The Information cites at least $7.5 billion in shipments. Neither number is confirmed as established fact, and reporting does not split them between legal and illegal routes.
No finding exists. The US investigation into alleged diversion or smuggling had not reached a conclusion in the cited reporting. Megaspeed and related parties deny any link to illegal diversion and say they have cooperated with US inspections.
Did Alibaba or Tencent knowingly take part in illegal diversion?
That claim is unconfirmed. Reports name Alibaba, Tencent and smaller Chinese AI laboratories as end users served by some of the chips, but being an end user does not establish knowledge of any illegal conduct.
Speedmatrix is a Malaysian subsidiary linked in reporting to Megaspeed's network. Its appearance in coverage reflects the regional footprint of the company, not a finding of wrongdoing.
Watch for any US rule on remote GPU access, new vetting requirements from Nvidia for cloud partners, and updates from the Megaspeed investigation. Any of those could change pricing and onboarding for cloud GPU rentals in Southeast Asia.

Congress moves to tighten AI chip export rules after Jensen Huang quits Nvidia
Four bills are circulating, from chip location tracking to a ban on renting overseas data centers. Republicans want them inside the must-pass defense authorization bill, while Colette Kress runs Nvidia as interim CEO and lawmakers press Commerce over enforcement on indirect shipments.

Nvidia spent years lobbying Washington against tighter chip curbs, and its CEO's exit has taken away its best lobbyist. If you build, buy or invest in AI hardware, the rules on who can import it are about to get less predictable.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said on November 12 that there is a "developing consensus in Congress" on limiting chip exports to China, according to Reuters. It came within a day of Nvidia announcing that Jensen Huang, its co-founder and chief executive for 33 years, had resigned as CEO and left the board, amid reports of a relationship with a woman US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing.
Republicans want to attach the new restrictions to the annual defense authorization bill, which Reuters described as a must-pass measure. That route matters more than any single bill. Standalone chip legislation has died before: Bloomberg reported in December 2025 that Congress rejected an effort to curb chip exports in what it called a lobbying win for Nvidia. Riding on the defense bill means the fight happens inside legislation that has to pass.
Reuters listed four proposals in play. The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more say over exports of advanced AI chips. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track where advanced processors end up, aimed at smuggling. The Remote Access Security Act would let the Commerce Department stop Chinese firms from renting data centers overseas to reach Nvidia hardware. The Match Act would push US allies to limit sales of chipmaking equipment to China.
Notice what the third one does. Today a Chinese lab that can't buy a chip can often rent time on one in another country. Closing that gap is a bigger change than another list of banned part numbers, and it lands on cloud providers as much as on chipmakers.
Nvidia tells cloud clients to cap China business at 49% of their services
Operators that buy Nvidia chips in bulk and rent out the compute are the ones affected. The guidance effectively asks them to send at least 51% of their services to firms outside China, and Nvidia reportedly passed it on verbally through sales and regional teams. - Nvidia China business restrictions for cloud providers - data center clients limiting Chinese customer revenue exposure
The politics changed because of how Huang left. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO and said it would search inside and outside the company for a permanent successor, according to NPR and Al Jazeera. DigitalToday reported that Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear in December and threatened subpoenas, while House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast said Huang agreed to testify. Reuters put his expected testimony before Thanksgiving on November 26. Those two timelines don't match, so expect the date to move.
DigitalToday also reported that lawmakers are scrutinizing a Singapore company, Megaspeed, suspected of smuggling restricted Nvidia chips into China, and criticism of Lutnick for delaying enforcement on indirect shipments. Commerce will want to answer the criticism of Lutnick. Frankly, a tracking mandate looks a lot more reasonable to a skeptical senator when the supposed gatekeepers are being asked why indirect shipments went unchecked.
Huang spent much of 2025 arguing that limits on sales to China would backfire, and he had the access to make that case in person. TechRadar covered his visits to Republicans and the Trump administration on exactly this. Kress has no such record on the Hill, and a company in the middle of a CEO search is poorly placed to start one.
Nvidia carries the obvious risk, and it has been here before. In April 2025 it took a $5.5 billion charge when the US required licences for its H20 chip in China, and AMD warned of a hit of up to $800 million. Neither company has said what the new bills would cost. Tracking requirements would add compliance work and could slow shipments to any buyer, not just Chinese ones, and that cost tends to end up in server prices.
Democrats signal broader action after they take the House majority in January 2027, DigitalToday reported, so this isn't a push that fades with the news cycle. If you buy GPUs in volume, plan on paperwork rather than a clean ban. If you sell them, the people who used to make your case in Washington are now answering questions in it.
Nvidia hasn't named a permanent CEO, and no vote on the defense bill's chip language has been scheduled.

Want to Invest in Top Growth Stocks Like Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft but Avoid Nvidia? Consider This Low-Cost Vanguard ETF That’s Up 24.8% This Year.
Investors who want to avoid Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) but put capital to work in growth-focused, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) face a difficult challenge. Nvidia is an integral part of index funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) -- as the second-largest S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) holding behind Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL). Nvidia also joined the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) in 2024. And Nvidia carries an especially high weighting in many growth ETFs and tech sector ETFs.
However, there is a unique low-cost Vanguard ETF that doesn't own Nvidia yet still holds Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Apple, and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) as its top three holdings.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF (NASDAQ:VONV) is a modern take on value stocks . While the Vanguard Growth ETF , Vanguard S&P 500 Growth ETF , and Vanguard Mega Cap Growth ETF label most major tech-focused companies as growth stocks, the Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF takes a nuanced approach.
The Russell 1000 is the 1,000 largest U.S. listed companies by market cap. It includes smaller large-cap and mid-cap stocks, whereas the S&P 500 just has large-cap stocks.
FTSE Russell, a subsidiary of the London Stock Exchange Group , has a semi-annual reconstitution whereby it roughly splits the market cap weighting of the Russell 1000 into two indexes -- the Russell 1000 Value Index (which the Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF tracks) and the Russell 1000 Growth Index -- which is mirrored by the Vanguard Russell 1000 Growth ETF . If FTSE Russell categorized all tech-focused companies as growth stocks, then the growth index would have a far higher market cap than the value index. So instead, FTSE Russell categorizes some established companies that were formerly high-octane growth stocks as value stocks, like Amazon, which is in the value index and not the growth index. Some stocks have their market caps split between both indexes. For example, Apple and Microsoft are top holdings in both indexes, whereas Nvidia, Alphabet, Broadcom , Meta Platforms , and Tesla -- among other names -- are solely in the growth index.
As a result, the Russell 1000 Value ETF's three largest holdings are Amazon, Apple, and Microsoft -- which make up a combined 17.4% of the ETF as of Sept. 30. Normally, Apple and Microsoft would have higher weightings than Amazon because they have higher market caps. But since all of Amazon's market cap is weighted exclusively by the value index while Apple and Microsoft are split, Amazon is actually the largest individual holding in the Russell 1000 Value ETF.
Other top holdings in the ETF are more traditional value stocks like Berkshire Hathaway , JPMorgan Chase , ExxonMobil , Johnson & Johnson , Intel , AbbVie , and Cisco Systems -- although I wouldn't be surprised if Intel and Cisco join the growth index during the next rebalancing.
The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF has a 21.6 price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio and 1.5% dividend yield, making it less expensive and more income-focused than the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF -- which has a 24 P/E and 1.1% yield. The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF has a dirt cheap fee structure -- charging a mere 0.06% expense ratio, or $6 for every $10,000 invested. The ETF has crushed the S&P 500 year to date, driven by strong performance in key value-focused sectors such as energy, consumer staples, and healthcare, and the ETF's lower exposure to the semiconductor industry relative to the S&P 500.
The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF is a top buy now
The Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF is a great buy for investors who view Amazon as an established cloud computing and retail giant, Apple as a modern-day consumer staple, and Microsoft as a balanced technology conglomerate with a clear runway for moderate earnings appreciation and a growing dividend. Even with these names, the ETF is more value-focused than the S&P 500. The ETF's 19.5% weighting in the technology sector makes it a nice middle ground between a more growth-focused index like the S&P 500 and traditional value ETFs that will exclude giant tech stocks like Apple and Microsoft.
All told, the Vanguard Russell 1000 Value ETF is the ideal fit for investors who want to buy an ETF with leading growth stocks but who are also satisfied with their existing Nvidia holdings or want to avoid the stock altogether.

items.content:
Anthropic IPO is make or break for the technology industry
Anthropic's IPO comes at a tough moment for the tech industry, which has been hammered by bad news, from struggling neoclouds to the crisis at Nvidia.
Leading chipmakers and internet giants need the IPO to go well, as Anthropic has $900 billion in spending commitments, including $110 billion over 10 years with Amazon.
"The numbers are just staggering," said Joe Fath, an investor at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, center, arrives near the White House ahead of a planned meeting with President Donald Trump in Washington on Sept. 29, 2026.
Between rising interest rates, a nationwide AI backlash, a major political shift in Washington, D.C., and the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , the tech industry is under mounting strain.
Now comes the most important tech IPO in years, and a defining event for the burgeoning but still young artificial intelligence market.
With Anthropic expected to debut on the Nasdaq on Thursday, the stakes are sky-high for almost every major tech company. Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , Google , Micron , Microsoft , Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company are collectively investing $26 billion at the IPO price, which is currently expected at $70 to $78 a share. Some of those companies are existing investors, as is early backer Amazon , whose stake could be in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
In addition to all the cash on the line, tech giants also need Anthropic's spending for many years to come. The Claude creator and its top rival, OpenAI, are driving an outsized amount of the AI buildout, and are burning historic amounts of money in the process.
Anthropic has outstanding spending commitments of over $900 billion, according to its latest prospectus . It's on the hook to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon over the course of a decade, and another $400 billion with other companies for cloud capacity, according to filings and partner disclosures. The lab also made $300 billion in commitments with data center and chip partners. Anthropic intends to lay out $125 billion to $150 billion for AI chips from Google , though delivery won't start until 2028.
"The numbers are just staggering," Joe Fath, a partner at venture firm Eclipse and former T. Rowe Price portfolio manager, said in an interview. "It's hard to get your head wrapped around it."
Cloud partners Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31% of contractual obligations, Anthropic said in its prospectus. Last year, Amazon built an Indiana data center just for Anthropic, using custom chips.
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy speaks during a keynote address at AWS re:Invent 2024, a conference hosted by Amazon Web Services, at The Venetian Las Vegas on December 3, 2024 in Las Vegas, Nevada.
By going public now, Anthropic can raise a large portion of the money it needs to pay for the technology and infrastructure required for building and hosting its frontier models and expanding portfolio of services. The company recorded a net loss of $104 billion through the first nine months of 2026. The IPO could yield over $90 billion in proceeds, on top of Anthropic's $132 billion in existing cash, including short-term investments.
The length of Anthropic's contracts is also unique. Typically such contracts last five years or less, while Anthropic's agreement with Amazon extends for twice that amount of time.
"Realistically, anything past three to four years, you're basically throwing darts in the dark," said Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at spend management software vendor Duckbill. "It is almost a certainty that it will be renegotiated long before the culmination of that contract."
Meanwhile, a data center for Anthropic that starts leasing in 2027 has a 20-year term. For both space and computing, Anthropic is splurging now so it doesn't end up short on capacity long into the future.
"In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment," Anthropic said in the prospectus.
Anthropic and Amazon didn't provide a comment.
It's a tough time for Anthropic to hit the Nasdaq, with the offering coming as tech investors are desperate for some good news. The Nasdaq is down to start November after dropping 5.3% in October, its worst month since March 2025.
Rising interest rates pushed investors out of debt-heavy neoclouds , which have become a critical piece of the infrastructure buildout. And in the midterm elections earlier this month, Democrats won sweeping victories in both houses of Congress and in key gubernatorial races, while dozens of ballot measures were passed that will potentially limit new data center development across the country.
Then came the Nvidia crisis. Shares of the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom tumbled 13% this week to their lowest since July 2025, after Huang's multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, led to his ouster early Thursday. Huang was replaced on an interim basis with CFO Colette Cress , who faces a major test on Tuesday, two days before the Anthropic debut, as Nvidia is set to report quarterly results.
The ongoing Nvidia fallout and the Anthropic IPO create quite the split-screen moment for tech's heavyweights, which are closely tied to both companies.
Google will be paying particularly close attention.
The company is set to own about 13% of Anthropic after the IPO, and is backstopping the lab's $19 billion in lease commitments to Terawulf , which will supply data center space in Kentucky. If Anthropic goes insolvent, Google will step in and pay the remaining rent or a termination fee, Terawulf said .
"Everybody knows that Anthropic is going to be the future of Google," said Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google cloud partnerships leader who now advises companies.
Experts assess the fallout from Nvidia's spy scandal and what it means for AI stocks
One major impetus for Anthropic to enter costly and long-term guarantees is that OpenAI is being equally aggressive, and capacity is limited, particularly for graphics processing units. Going long can mean locking in rates as the industry confronts questions about whether data center development will slow.
"You will need to be in a rush to get infrastructure, and if you are not going to be there, you will be out of business," said Eli Mansoor, CEO of OskaQ Consulting, which advises companies on cloud negotiations. "It used to be that prices always go down, but this is changing, especially in the GPU world."
Big financial firms are lining up to help Anthropic get what it wants. Bank of America , Blackstone , Citigroup and Morgan Stanley have offered $63 billion to buy racks full of Broadcom AI chips that Anthropic will rent. Broadcom has provided a backstop with a maximum liability of $43 billion .
That's a lot of silicon and a massive bet for a five-year-old company that's never lived through a technology downturn.
"It's not a risk-free prospect, but I would call it smart investing," said David Tollen, founder of Sycamore Legal, where he specializes in IT contracts. "They're investing, in a sense, in themselves. They're putting money into something that if it succeeds, they get a piece of the action."

Apple Black Friday Starts Early: Save on Apple Watch, MacBook Air, and More
Sunday November 15, 2026 10:02 am PST by Mitchel Broussard
Black Friday is now less than two weeks away, taking place on Friday, November 27 in 2026. As always, this will be the best time of the year to shop for great deals, including popular Apple products like AirPods, iPad, Apple Watch, and more.
Note: MacRumors is an affiliate partner with some of these vendors. When you click a link and make a purchase, we may receive a small payment, which helps us keep the site running.
Specifically, in this article we're sharing all of the Apple products that currently have all-time low prices, or discounts that are at least close to their record-low prices. Of course, these are early Black Friday deals, so even better discounts could emerge later in the month, but if you're shopping right now these are all the best prices around.
You can use the links below to jump directly to the section you're shopping for today.
Notable AirPods deals this month include solid second-best prices on the AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2, with up to $100 off these models.
You can get the 42mm GPS Apple Watch Series 12 for $329.00 at Amazon and the 46mm GPS model for $379.00 at Best Buy, both of which are $70 discounts and new all-time low prices. Amazon's selection of colors and styles is limited as of writing, while Best Buy has more options on sale .
Amazon also has both Dark Bronze Milanese Loop models on sale for new record low prices today, starting at $379.00 for the 42mm GPS model and increasing to $429.00 for the 46mm GPS model.

We've created a big list of more Apple Watch Series 12 models on sale below, including Titanium and Ceramic options at new best-ever prices. Remember that Best Buy is matching these deals as well if you prefer to shop there.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 has dropped to $699.99 on Amazon in one of the most notable early Black Friday discounts, down from $799.00. This is a match of the all-time low price on the new Ultra 4, which just launched in September.
If you're shopping for a Milanese Loop model, Amazon also has a $99 discount on one of these devices. There are five regular models on sale and two Milanese Loop models, and most have delivery dates of early November on Amazon.
Regarding the previous-generation models, Best Buy this week has a big collection of Apple Watch Ultra 3 models for $549.00, down from $799.00. This is a massive $250 discount on the previous-generation device, and it represents a new all-time low price on these models.
Apple's AirTag 2 has hit $23.00 this week on Amazon, down from $29.00. This deal is on the 1-Pack of the AirTag 2, and it's an all-time low price.
Apple's new Mac mini has had one of the most consistent discounts over the past few weeks, and these $119-$150 markdowns have continued into Black Friday season. Prices start at $779.00 for the entry-level model, and currently include every M6 model, plus the M5 Pro model.
Additionally, one of the best early Black Friday deals is on the M5 Max Mac Studio with 36GB RAM and a 512GB SSD, on sale for $2,299.00, down from $2,499.00.
Amazon is taking $199 off nearly every model of the M5 MacBook Air this week, with matches of the best post-hike prices we've ever seen on the computer. Prices now start at $1,099.99 for the 512GB 13-inch model and $1,299.99 for the 512GB 15-inch model.
For the 15-inch M5 MacBook Air models, prices start with the 16GB/512GB model for $1,299.00, down from $1,499.00. You can also get the 16GB/1TB model for $1,549.99, down from $1,799.00, which is a $250 markdown and another all-time low price for Black Friday.
Cellular carriers have always offered big savings on the newest iPhone models during the holidays, and Black Friday 2026 sales have kicked off at AT&T and T-Mobile , as well as Best Buy . Right now we're tracking notable offers on the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo. For even more savings, keep an eye on older models during the holiday shopping season.
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max : Up to $1,200 off with eligible trade-in
iPhone Duo : Up to $1,200 off with eligible trade-in
Apple Watch SE 3: No cost (up to $300) when adding a watch line on a qualifying plan, or get $250 off any Apple Watch when picking up another Apple Watch
T-Mobile is offering the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max for up to $1,200 off when you trade in an old device (in any condition) and purchase the new device on an eligible unlimited plan. You can also get this offer if you switch a line to Experience Beyond 2.0, Experience Beyond, or Go5G Next.
For anyone shopping for the iPhone Duo, you can get up to $1,200 off the iPhone Duo with any condition trade-in on an Experience Beyond plan. This discount will appear in the form of bill credits over the course of 36 months.
Similarly, if you're on the Experience More or Experience Beyond plan, you can get up to $830 off with a trade-in, and up to $730 off with a new line on most other plans. All of these offers have the same payout schedule over the course of 36 months.
iPhone 18 Pro Max : Up to $1,200 off with eligible trade-in
iPhone Duo : Up to $1,200 off with eligible trade-in
Over at AT&T , you can get the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max for up to $1,200 off with an iPhone trade-in in any condition. You'll need to upgrade with AT&T Next Up Anytime or switch to get this offer.
Additionally, new and existing customers can get up to $1,200 off the iPhone Duo with an eligible trade-in. If you're switching to AT&T, the carrier will give you up to $800 to pay off your current device balance, and you can save $200 per line when ordering the smartphone online.
In regards to the main offer of up to $1,200 off the iPhone Duo, AT&T says this requires an eligible trade-in of $230 or more, alongside activation of a new line or upgrading an existing line. You'll get this credit over the course of 36 months on your AT&T bill.
You can find the breakdown of each plan tier from AT&T below, and remember that they each require a trade-in as well.
Up to $1,200 off iPhone Duo: requires AT&T Premium 2.0 plan or higher / trade-in value of $230 or more
Up to $930 off iPhone Duo: requires AT&T Extra 2.0 plan or higher / trade-in value of $130 or more
Up to $500 off iPhone Duo: requires Value 2.0 plan / trade-in value of $130 or more
Up to $350 off iPhone Duo: requires any eligible unlimited plan / trade-in value of $35-$129
If you switch to AT&T from a different carrier, AT&T will pay off your phone balance at up to $800 off per line. With the $1,200 offer, AT&T is offering the 256GB iPhone 18 Pro at no cost.
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max : Up to $1,200 off with qualified activation and trade-in
iPhone Duo : Up to $1,200 off with qualified activation and trade-in
Carriers aren't the only place you can save on iPhones this year, with Best Buy offering the same discounts as AT&T and T-Mobile with activation through these carriers at the time of purchase. This is a great option for anyone who shops at Best Buy a lot and likes to rack up member reward points.
Similar to the carriers, you can get the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo for up to $1,200 off with qualified activation on cellular plans and a trade-in of an older device. Best Buy supports activation through AT&T and Verizon.
Amazon this week has big discounts across Apple's Clear, Silicone, and TechWoven Cases for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup. Across the board these are the best prices we've tracked to date on the new cases for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. This time around the deals do not require any coupon codes to see the final sale prices.

If you're on the hunt for protection for your new iPhone Duo, we've also been keeping track of all the best cases and screen protectors for the new device. The catch with these accessories is that many of them are not on sale given how new the Duo is, but there are overall cheap options you can find on Amazon, plus a great buy two get 20% off deal at ZAGG.
Amazon has some notable TechWoven dupe cases on sale, available for $32.99 , which is $50 cheaper than any of Apple's official iPhone Duo cases. Otherwise, you'll find the full list of retailers offering accessories for the iPhone Duo below.

If you’re promoting Apple again this year with their gift cards, I’m going to lose it.
It’s one thing to declare Black Friday the biggest holiday of the year. Do whatever you want, it’s your call. I’d rather celebrate Christmas.
But Apple doesn’t participate in Black Friday. Apple doesn’t offer discounts. The company never has.
So that the customer is forced to buy from Apple again. To pay the inflated prices and to do so willingly, no less.
Yes, mention it. But please, I’m asking you, don’t praise Apple again for its gift cards.
Instead, point out critically that anyone who buys products on Black Friday from them is committing sacrilege on this holy holiday.
You can typically get those prices any day of the week at Costco
Not only has Black Friday gone from a day to a week to now a month of deals, the “deals” are just the same sales we get all year round anyway.
Also there’s the conditioning of an underlying belief that we can “save more and more and more” by spending more and more and more. No. The best savings are by not spending at all.
